title: Terminal Screenreader Mode
user: Blind and low-vision developers who need noisy streaming CLI output to remain intelligible and navigable in NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Linux gamer built a select-to-speak overlay because existing tools could not read arbitrary game and video text quickly enough.
38 reactions and 64 comments request a screen-reader flag that removes spinners, ANSI output, and rapidly rewritten streaming text that can freeze readers.

recurrence: Independent 2025–26 requests identify the same failure mode: dynamic visual/terminal output becomes unusable when it changes in place; it blocks work rather than merely inconveniencing users.
current_workaround: Restart the screen reader or terminal, copy output into a text editor, or avoid streaming interfaces.
incumbents_and_gap: Terminal emulators, NVDA, JAWS, and individual tools' accessibility modes help inconsistently; there is no small cross-CLI adapter that turns volatile output into a stable semantic transcript.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI wrapper that detects ANSI rewrites and spinners, emits a linear timestamped transcript, exposes headings/links, and offers optional earcons. Non-goals: a terminal emulator, cloud transcription, or an AI coding agent.
success_measure: In a five-task screen-reader pilot, 8 of 10 participants complete streamed-command reading without restarting their reader or losing their place.
monetization: free — trust and compatibility require a no-account local tool; paid enterprise support is optional later.
constraints: Must not log commands or output by default; preserve Unicode safely; test with NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, and common shells; earcons need an off switch.
why_distinct: It normalizes volatile terminal rendering into an accessibility surface, rather than adding another speech engine or terminal.

title: Stream Reader Compass
user: Screen-reader users working with long, streaming AI or support chats who need to read, copy, and act on a conversation without focus loss.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN requester wants a local, background meeting transcript pipeline because existing transcription products do not fit a durable, controllable workflow.
44 reactions and 44 comments describe static accessible chat views that lose place, expose links as text, and interrupt readers during streaming.

recurrence: Both threads seek a durable linear record instead of an opaque live surface; focus loss and uncopyable output make an otherwise useful workflow inaccessible.
current_workaround: Open a separate accessible view, copy fragments to a document, or repeatedly restart navigation from the latest answer.
incumbents_and_gap: VS Code Accessible View and chat apps expose app-specific controls; none provides a privacy-preserving reader-first transcript layer that can be used across browser chat surfaces.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension that, on user command, creates a local semantic transcript with message headings, stable anchors, copy/export, link buttons, and polite update cues. Non-goals: model access, summarization, or recording private conversations by default.
success_measure: At least 70% of pilot sessions use heading navigation or resume markers, and users rate loss-of-place incidents below one per hour.
monetization: free — a narrowly scoped assistive layer needs trust and broad adoption before any paid support offering.
constraints: Process page content locally; require an explicit per-site enablement; respect CSP and browser-extension permissions; no telemetry of conversation text.
why_distinct: The value is continuity and semantic navigation of existing streams, not generating another chat transcript with an LLM.

title: Local Live Captions
user: Deaf and hard-of-hearing students on Linux who need captions for lectures, video calls, and recordings when hosts did not enable captions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A requester trying to make a simple live transcript for a NASA stream reports that the source's captions are difficult to access programmatically.
A hearing-disabled university user says Zoom, Teams, Discord, and recordings often lack usable captions, forcing an hour of manual Whisper work or booting Windows.

recurrence: Live and recorded speech remains captionless outside the largest platforms; the reported workaround consumes an hour per recording and does not solve live calls.
current_workaround: Ask hosts to enable captions, manually download recordings and run Whisper, or switch operating systems.
incumbents_and_gap: Windows Live Captions is useful but platform-bound; unmaintained Linux projects and web-call captions do not cover arbitrary system audio with language choice and local retention.
smallest_useful_product: An offline Linux desktop overlay for selected system-audio input with downloadable speech models, English/German first, adjustable caption size, and transcript export. Non-goals: meeting bots, cloud recording, speaker surveillance, or perfect diarization.
success_measure: At least 75% of 20-minute pilot recordings yield captions users keep enabled through the session, with no audio uploaded off-device.
monetization: one-time — downloadable local models and an offline utility have clear value without recurring audio-data costs.
constraints: Obtain consent before captioning calls; make capture state obvious; model licenses and multilingual accuracy must be verified; avoid storing audio by default.
why_distinct: It is a consent-forward, local system-audio caption overlay for the gaps between platforms, not another meeting recorder.

title: Caption Layout Keeper
user: Caption users watching educational and dialogue-heavy video who need speaker, position, emphasis, and collision-avoidance information to survive playback.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A report says YouTube disabled advanced SRV3 subtitling and is stripping formatting from older videos, including positioning, speaker color, and styling.
11 reactions request enhanced captions because plain bottom-fixed text obscures content and loses speaker distinction, positioning, size, and pronunciation cues.

recurrence: Two independent reports identify format loss—not absence of transcript text—as the accessibility failure; the missing layout changes meaning and hides visual content.
current_workaround: Use a platform's plain captions, rely on the video image, or download and manually style subtitle files where possible.
incumbents_and_gap: YouTube and SmartTube support basic captions; their rendering is platform-dependent and authors cannot preview a resilient fallback that retains meaningful cues.
smallest_useful_product: A local caption-file viewer/converter that preserves WebVTT/SRV-style positioning where possible and emits an accessible fallback with speaker labels, cue descriptions, and collision warnings. Non-goals: downloading copyrighted videos, hosting captions, or automatic translation.
success_measure: In a 30-file corpus, users can identify the intended speaker and avoid on-screen-text collisions in at least 90% of annotated cues.
monetization: free — caption interoperability benefits from open formats and must not gate access to accessibility content.
constraints: Operate only on user-provided caption files; preserve source attribution; do not bypass platform controls or redistribute copyrighted media; test RTL and CJK text.
why_distinct: It protects semantic caption layout and creates a graceful accessible fallback, rather than being a video downloader or generic subtitle editor.

title: Caption Choice Memory
user: Caption-dependent video viewers who need their language and auto-caption preferences to be reachable in one action and retained per site/device.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user must scroll through a long language list every time to reach English subtitles.
A separate playback request asks for an option to disable automatic captions when videos turn them on unexpectedly.

recurrence: Opposite default needs—always show a chosen language versus never auto-enable—show that caption preference is personal and currently too expensive to express repeatedly.
current_workaround: Scroll language menus, toggle captions video by video, or tolerate an unwanted default.
incumbents_and_gap: Platform menus offer many languages but do not consistently pin a preferred ordered set or expose a predictable caption policy across embedded players.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension with a per-site caption policy: prefer language list, enable/disable default, single keyboard shortcut, and clear unsupported-player notice. Non-goals: subtitle downloading, translation, or modifying DRM playback.
success_measure: Pilot users reduce median actions from page load to their desired caption state to one or fewer on supported players.
monetization: free — the narrow preference utility has no service cost and should be frictionless for caption users.
constraints: Use only documented/player DOM controls; no circumvention of DRM or platform controls; store preferences locally and provide a visible per-site off switch.
why_distinct: It is an accessibility preference router, not a caption generator or another video platform.

title: Color Signal Lens
user: People with color-vision differences who need software status, diffs, and charts to remain distinguishable without globally distorting their screen.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A technical user says OS and game color-correction options do not cover the full spectrum of color blindness and investigates ICC profiles.
15 reactions report red/green code diffs that are hard or impossible to distinguish and request contrast plus accessible presets.

recurrence: A system-level correction gap and a concrete high-frequency diff task independently show that color-only signals persist despite built-in filters.
current_workaround: Enable broad OS filters, change app themes where available, or infer meaning from position and text.
incumbents_and_gap: OS color filters affect everything; apps may offer themes but lack a quick, task-specific way to reveal semantic red/green signals while maintaining the rest of a user's display.
smallest_useful_product: A desktop color-picker/lens that samples a selected region and overlays configurable patterns, labels, or blue/orange remapping for detected status colors. Non-goals: medical diagnosis, whole-screen color management, or modifying other apps' data.
success_measure: In a blinded diff-identification test, participants improve add/remove classification accuracy by 25 percentage points over their baseline theme.
monetization: one-time — an offline utility has no meaningful recurring operating cost.
constraints: Never claim to correct vision; screenshot permission must be transparent and on-demand; overlays must not capture or upload screen content; test multiple color-vision simulations.
why_distinct: It makes color-only status legible at the moment of work, instead of applying a blunt global screen filter.

title: Voice Line Navigator
user: Windows voice-access users editing large text files who need reliable spoken movement to visible, addressable lines without mouse precision.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A mobile voice user asks why a capable voice interface cannot control their phone and says they would pay for control.
20 reactions request exposed line numbers so Windows Voice Access can understand a spoken 'go to line x' command in the editor.

recurrence: These requests are not for novelty dictation: users need voice to act on real interface targets, especially exact navigation targets that are invisible to accessibility APIs.
current_workaround: Use keyboard shortcuts, dictate imprecisely, or rely on mouse/another person for navigation.
incumbents_and_gap: Windows Voice Access and editor shortcuts exist, but commands fail when line/address metadata is not exposed or varies across apps.
smallest_useful_product: A Windows accessibility helper with explicit hotkeys and spoken commands for next/previous line, line number, selection, and jump-to-line in supported plain-text editors. Non-goals: general phone control, background microphone collection, or remote automation.
success_measure: Supported-editor pilots complete a 15-location navigation script with at least 90% successful spoken jumps and no touch/mouse interaction.
monetization: free — the initial accessibility integration needs community validation and cannot depend on speech-data monetization.
constraints: Push-to-talk by default; local recognition where possible; require explicit app support rather than synthetic clicks into arbitrary UI; avoid sending code/audio to a server.
why_distinct: It supplies a narrow, verifiable semantic navigation bridge instead of promising unsafe universal voice control.

title: Project Color Beacons
user: Dyslexic and ADHD developers juggling several similar windows who need an immediate non-text cue for which project they are about to edit.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A team asks how to support a careful colleague whose suspected dyslexia-related typos escape reviews and have caused production outages.
A dyslexic/ADHD developer explains that identical project windows cause wrong-repo edits and requests per-project chrome colors; text labels are not sufficient.

recurrence: The reports connect cognitive load to real errors: one asks for a respectful prevention mechanism, the other names project identity as a repeated focus failure.
current_workaround: Read title bars repeatedly, use manually customized editor settings, or make avoidable cross-project mistakes.
incumbents_and_gap: VS Code/Cursor workspace colors and Peacock help one editor; there is no lightweight cross-app visual identity convention for project folders and windows.
smallest_useful_product: A local desktop helper plus editor configs that assigns a stable high-contrast color/name/icon beacon per project root and shows a confirmation strip before focus-sensitive actions. Non-goals: diagnosing dyslexia/ADHD, task management, or employee monitoring.
success_measure: In a multi-project task test, participants reduce wrong-window edits by 50% compared with identical-window baseline.
monetization: one-time — a private, local accommodation utility should not require an ongoing subscription.
constraints: Color cannot be the sole cue; include text/icon alternatives and color-blind palettes; project paths remain local; integrations must use supported editor APIs.
why_distinct: It treats visual project identity as an error-prevention accommodation rather than another focus timer or theme pack.

title: Read Along Queue
user: Readers with attention or reading-access needs who want selected web articles spoken aloud in a controlled queue without surrendering reading history to a cloud service.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A current e-reader buyer crowdsources options around screen size, buttons, writing, backlight, and ecosystem—evidence that reading hardware workflows remain fragmented.
24 reactions request integrated text-to-speech and speech-to-text in a local-document application rather than a separate service.

recurrence: Users are actively assembling personal reading systems and ask for speech inside their local document flow, not merely another generic TTS API.
current_workaround: Switch among an e-reader, browser reader mode, OS TTS, and commercial read-later subscriptions.
incumbents_and_gap: Pocket-like readers, Speechify, OS TTS, and e-readers cover pieces of the flow; few provide an offline-first, keyboard-friendly queue that follows a reader's own web selections.
smallest_useful_product: A local-first browser extension/PWA that extracts user-selected readable text, queues it, drives system voices, tracks position, and exports an open bookmark list. Non-goals: voice cloning, publishing audio, AI summaries, or cloud account sync in v1.
success_measure: At least half of pilot users resume three or more queued readings in the following week without re-finding their place.
monetization: free — use system voices and local storage; no speech data or reading history needs to fund the product.
constraints: Only process user-selected pages; honor site content restrictions; no scraping paywalled text; provide dyslexia-friendly visual controls and a fully keyboard-operable player.
why_distinct: The unit is a private, resumable read-along queue, not an LLM summary or a cloud voice subscription.

title: Keyboard Route Check
user: Keyboard-only users and small web teams who need to prove the route through an interactive page is coherent before it becomes a production accessibility defect.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer considering a JavaScript-heavy interactive blog explicitly worries it will be an accessibility nightmare and asks for an approach that respects humans.
27 reactions report mouse-only controls, unfocusable elements, and broken tab/reverse-tab behavior in a widely used date picker.

recurrence: The design-stage concern and a concrete component failure show that keyboard routes are missed before release and costly to reconstruct later.
current_workaround: Manually tab through a page, run a generic accessibility scanner, or find the problem after keyboard users report it.
incumbents_and_gap: axe and Lighthouse catch important static rules; browser devtools show accessibility trees, but neither makes the actual tab journey, focus escape, and reverse path a small reviewable artifact.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension that records a user-run Tab/Shift+Tab path, names each focused element, flags loops/skips/invisible focus, and exports a shareable route report. Non-goals: automatic WCAG certification, synthetic browser testing, or replacing manual testing.
success_measure: In pilot audits, teams identify a previously unknown focus-order defect on at least 30% of tested interactive pages.
monetization: freemium — free single-page reports build adoption; paid team history and CI export can support maintenance.
constraints: Record labels/roles rather than page text where possible; redact form values; do not claim compliance; respect pages with sensitive data.
why_distinct: It turns a human keyboard journey into evidence, not another static lint wrapper.

title: Screenreader Task Audit
user: Blind founders and small product teams who need to demonstrate whether essential dashboard tasks can actually be completed with a screen reader.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN explicitly solicits the worst accessibility experiences people have encountered, indicating active frustration with inaccessible sites.
23 reactions: a visually impaired entrepreneur cannot use analytics tasks with a screen reader and says automated tools fall short for interactive scenarios.

recurrence: The most severe gap is task completion, not a score: a business owner is blocked from their own analytics despite generic automated testing.
current_workaround: Run automated scans, ask a consultant for a broad audit, or rely on sighted colleagues to complete essential tasks.
incumbents_and_gap: axe, Lighthouse, and enterprise audit services are valuable but do not create a repeatable, lightweight task script with tester-observed announcements, focus, and blockers.
smallest_useful_product: A privacy-preserving web app that lets a team define five critical tasks, captures a screen-reader tester's structured observations and optional local event trace, then outputs a prioritized reproducible report. Non-goals: automated accessibility certification, remote surveillance, or synthetic speech testing.
success_measure: Teams using it reproduce and fix at least one task-blocking issue within 14 days in 60% of pilot audits.
monetization: freemium — a free small audit supports access; paid collaborative reports and retention support teams.
constraints: Never capture passwords, analytics payloads, or page text by default; obtain tester consent; make reports WCAG-informed but not legal advice; support anonymized exports.
why_distinct: It centers lived task evidence from a screen-reader user, filling the gap automated scanners explicitly cannot cover.

title: Silent Focus Sentinel
user: Mobile app teams and VoiceOver users who need to catch focus stops that announce nothing before a release makes navigation confusing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer asks for private, local tools that capture both the screen and accessibility tree to analyze work without exposing data.
38 reactions and 36 comments report an extra silent VoiceOver focus before the first list item, forcing a confusing additional swipe.

recurrence: A specific high-impact silent-stop regression and a separate demand for local accessibility-tree capture point to a missing debugging primitive, not a hypothetical feature.
current_workaround: Manually swipe every screen with VoiceOver, record a video, and inspect platform accessibility tools after a user finds a regression.
incumbents_and_gap: Xcode/Accessibility Inspector and framework test tools expose pieces of the tree but do not make a simple recorded sequence of focus target, label, role, and silence obvious in CI review.
smallest_useful_product: An iOS simulator-focused CLI that records a scripted focus traversal, flags focusable nodes with empty/duplicate announcements, and emits a compact JSON/HTML diff. Non-goals: a full mobile test framework, physical-device automation, or uploading app screens.
success_measure: On a seeded regression suite, it flags at least 90% of intentional empty-focus stops with fewer than 10% false positives.
monetization: free — a transparent open developer utility is the credible path for accessibility regression detection.
constraints: Simulator and OS accessibility APIs may limit coverage; keep artifacts local; label heuristics must allow intentionally decorative nodes; avoid claims of WCAG conformance.
why_distinct: It tests the sequence a screen-reader user experiences—especially silence—not merely whether accessibility attributes exist.
